analogy.p: Think of healthy tissue as a neat flower bed in which each plant grows only to its proper size and the gardener (the cell's control genes) removes any that grow out of place. A **benign tumour** is like a thick clump of weeds that stays inside its own bed, fenced in by a border: it takes up space but does not move. A **malignant tumour** is like weeds that **send seeds on the wind to other beds** and take root there, which is why it is so much harder to deal with. The analogy breaks down because weeds are a different species from the garden plants, whereas a tumour starts from the body's **own cells**, which have been changed by mutation.

bullets: **Cancer** = changes in cells that lead to **uncontrolled growth and division**.
**Benign tumour** = abnormal cells **contained in one area**, usually **within a membrane**; they do **not invade** other parts of the body.
**Malignant tumour** = cells **invade neighbouring tissues** and **spread to different parts of the body in the blood**, where they form **secondary tumours**.
**Lifestyle risk factors** have been identified for various types of cancer (for example smoking, obesity, alcohol, UV and other radiation).
**Genetic risk factors** exist for some cancers (for example inherited faulty versions of the genes **BRCA1 and BRCA2**, linked to breast and ovarian cancer).
Cancer is a **non-communicable disease**: you cannot catch it from another person (although some viruses raise the risk of certain cancers).
Link to other topics: mitosis and the cell cycle (4.1.2), stem cells, risk factors and non-communicable disease (4.2.2), screening and treatment in the wider course.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA expects you to **describe cancer as the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division**, and to **explain the difference between benign and malignant tumours**. You must also know that **scientists have identified lifestyle risk factors for various types of cancer** and that **there are also genetic risk factors for some cancers**. The topic sits inside the 'health and disease' content of Organisation, so it connects directly to risk factors, non-communicable diseases, mitosis and the cell cycle. Exam questions are typically 2 to 4 marks on definitions and comparisons, plus data questions on risk factors.

bullets: Mitosis produces **two genetically identical daughter cells** and is part of the **cell cycle** (growth, DNA replication, mitosis, cytokinesis).
Cells divide when needed: **growth** (embryo to adult), **repair** (healing a cut) and **replacement** (skin, gut lining, blood).
Genes code for **proteins that control the cell cycle**; these work like brakes and accelerators on division.
In healthy tissue, division **stops** once the tissue is repaired or the correct number of cells is reached.
Healthy cells are **differentiated**: they have the structure and sub-cellular structures for one job (for example a lung cell or a skin cell).
Cells that are damaged beyond repair are normally removed rather than allowed to divide.
If the control genes are damaged, the cell can lose its ability to stop dividing: this is the starting point for cancer.
core.h: Normal cell division is tightly controlled
core.p: To understand cancer you first need to remember how healthy tissue works. In a healthy body, cells divide by **mitosis** only when more cells are needed, for example to **grow**, or to **repair** damage and **replace** worn-out cells. Whether a cell divides is controlled by the **genes** in its DNA, which switch cell division on and off at the right time. This keeps every tissue at the correct size and shape, and keeps the cells specialised for their job.

bullets: The change happens in a **single cell**, but its descendants all inherit the faulty genes because mitosis makes **genetically identical** copies.
The cells divide **faster and for longer** than healthy cells, and often **fail to differentiate properly**.
Mutations can arise by chance when DNA is copied (copying errors) or be caused by **carcinogens** and **ionising radiation**.
Mutations that cause cancer affect genes controlling **when a cell divides**; they are not usually inherited, except in the cases of inherited risk genes.
Because each division doubles the number of cells, numbers rise **exponentially** (1, 2, 4, 8 ... 2 to the power n).
Cancer cells keep taking nutrients and oxygen from the blood, which can harm the surrounding healthy tissue.
A cancer is therefore a disease of **cell division**, not an infection by a pathogen.
core.h: What goes wrong in cancer: mutation and uncontrolled division
core.p: Cancer starts when a **change (mutation) in the DNA of a cell** affects the genes that control cell division. A **mutation** is a change in the sequence of bases in DNA. Usually a single mutation is not enough: several changes in the same cell line usually build up before cells escape control. The affected cell then **divides again and again by mitosis**, ignoring the signals that would normally tell it to stop, and each daughter cell inherits the same faulty genes. This **uncontrolled growth and division** is the defining feature of cancer.

bullets: A **tumour** is a mass of cells produced by uncontrolled division.
A tumour may press on nearby organs, nerves or blood vessels, causing symptoms (for example pain or blockage).
Tumours can be found in almost any tissue: skin, lung, bowel, breast, prostate, blood-forming tissue and so on.
The first tumour to form is the **primary tumour**; any new tumours formed elsewhere are **secondary tumours**.
Some cancers of the blood (leukaemia) do not form a single solid lump, but the idea of uncontrolled division is the same.
A tumour needs a **blood supply** to keep growing, because its cells need oxygen and glucose for respiration.
Do not call every lump a cancer: many lumps are benign or are not tumours at all.
core.h: Tumours: a mass of abnormal cells
core.p: The uncontrolled division of the abnormal cells produces a lump called a **tumour**. Tumours grow because more cells are produced than are lost. Not every tumour is dangerous: it depends whether the cells stay put or spread. Doctors therefore classify tumours as **benign** or **malignant**.

bullets: Cells are **contained in one area**, often **surrounded by a membrane** (a capsule).
They **do not invade** neighbouring tissue and **do not spread** to other parts of the body.
They do **not form secondary tumours**.
Growth is usually **slow**.
Usually **not life-threatening**, and often removed if they cause pressure or other problems.
Examples used in teaching: a wart or a fatty lump under the skin (a lipoma).
Exam wording to use: 'benign tumours are contained in one area, usually within a membrane, and do not invade other parts of the body'.
core.p: A **benign tumour** is a growth of abnormal cells which is **contained in one area, usually within a membrane**. The cells divide in an uncontrolled way, but they **do not invade other parts of the body**. Because they stay in one place, they are usually **not dangerous** and can often be removed by surgery. They can still cause problems if they grow large and press on organs or block a passage, which is why some are treated.

bullets: Cells **invade neighbouring tissues** instead of staying in one area.
Cells **spread to different parts of the body in the blood** (via the circulatory system).
They **form secondary tumours** in other organs (for example the lungs, liver or bones).
They are **dangerous** and can be **life-threatening**, especially once they have spread.
Treatment is more difficult once there are **several tumours**, which is why **early detection** matters.
A malignant tumour usually has no clear membrane, so its edge is **irregular**.
Exam wording to use: 'cells invade neighbouring tissues and spread to other parts of the body in the blood, forming secondary tumours'.
core.p: In a **malignant tumour** the cells **invade neighbouring tissues**. Some cells break away from the primary tumour, enter the **blood** (and, in reality, lymph), travel around the body and **spread to different parts of the body, where they form secondary tumours**. Spreading like this is often called **metastasis**, though the specification just says 'spread'. Malignant tumours are **cancers**: they are far more dangerous because they damage the surrounding tissues and can grow in several organs at once, making them harder to treat.

bullets: **Position:** benign cells stay in **one area**, usually within a membrane; malignant cells **invade neighbouring tissue**.
**Spread:** benign tumours **do not spread**; malignant cells **spread in the blood** to other parts of the body.
**Secondary tumours:** benign tumours **do not** form them; malignant tumours **do**.
**Danger:** benign tumours are **usually not dangerous**; malignant tumours are **cancers** and are dangerous.
**Treatment:** benign tumours are often removed or left alone; malignant tumours usually need more intense treatment.
**Similarity:** both are caused by **uncontrolled cell division** and both are a mass of abnormal cells.
**Edges:** benign tumours usually have a **smooth, defined edge**; malignant tumours have an **irregular edge** and invade surrounding tissue.
core.p: Examiners often ask you to **compare** the two types of tumour, so it is worth learning a point-by-point table in words. Always make sure both tumours are mentioned in each comparison sentence, using linking words such as 'whereas' or 'but'. A list of facts about only one tumour does not score as a comparison. The key differences are about **where the cells stay**, **whether they invade**, and **whether they spread to form secondary tumours**.

bullets: **Smoking** is a risk factor for **lung cancer** (and several other cancers); tar and other chemicals in smoke are **carcinogens**.
**Obesity** is a risk factor for several cancers, such as bowel and breast cancer in later life.
**Alcohol** is a risk factor for cancers such as liver and mouth cancer.
**UV radiation** from the sun or sunbeds is a risk factor for **skin cancer** because UV damages DNA.
**Ionising radiation** (for example X-rays, gamma rays, radioactive materials) can cause mutations that lead to cancer.
Some **viral infections** raise the risk of particular cancers (for example HPV and cervical cancer, hepatitis B and liver cancer).
A **balanced diet, exercise, not smoking, moderate alcohol and sun protection** lower the chance of developing cancer.
core.p: A **risk factor** is something that **increases the chance** of a person developing a disease; it does not guarantee that the disease will happen. Scientists have **identified lifestyle risk factors for various types of cancer** by comparing large groups of people and finding patterns in who becomes ill. Many cancer-causing agents are **carcinogens**, substances or types of radiation that can cause mutations in DNA. Most of these risks can be reduced by changing behaviour, which is why public health campaigns focus on them.

bullets: Genetic risk factors are **inherited**, so they are present from birth in every cell.
**BRCA1 and BRCA2** faulty alleles are linked to a higher risk of **breast and ovarian cancer** (and some other cancers).
People with a **family history** of certain cancers may be offered **genetic testing** and extra screening.
Inheriting the faulty gene gives a **higher chance**, not a certainty, of cancer.
Many cancers are **not** inherited: most mutations that cause cancer arise during a person's life.
Cancer often results from an **interaction of several factors**: genes, lifestyle and environment.
Ethical issues of testing include **anxiety**, **insurance and privacy**, and whether to choose **preventive surgery**.
core.p: For some cancers there is also a **genetic risk factor**, meaning that the person has **inherited a faulty version of a gene** that makes cancer more likely. The example named in the AQA specification is **BRCA1 and BRCA2**: these are genes normally involved in controlling cell division and repairing DNA, and faulty alleles of them are linked to **breast and ovarian cancer**. Having the inherited gene change **does not mean the person will definitely develop cancer**; it raises the chance. This is why genetic risk factors, like lifestyle ones, are about **probability**, not certainty.

bullets: **Correlation** = a link or pattern between two variables; **causation** = one variable actually causes the change in the other.
A larger **sample size** and a **long study period** make conclusions more reliable.
Look for a **dose effect**: more cigarettes per day tends to give a higher risk, which supports causation.
A **mechanism** (carcinogens cause mutations in genes controlling cell division) strengthens the claim.
Risk factors **increase the chance**, but not everyone exposed gets cancer, and some unexposed people do.
Be careful with words: say 'is linked to' or 'increases the risk of', not 'always causes'.
A **control group** or comparison with non-smokers is needed to judge the effect of smoking.
core.h: Correlation and causation: how we know a risk factor is real
core.p: Questions often give you data about a risk factor, such as the percentage of smokers and non-smokers who develop lung cancer. A **correlation** means that two things change together; it does **not on its own prove that one causes the other**. Scientists accept that a factor causes cancer when there is a **correlation** in large studies **and** a plausible **mechanism** (for example, chemicals in tobacco smoke damage DNA, causing mutations). Another factor, such as diet or occupation, could create a misleading link, which is why careful studies compare similar groups.

bullets: **Percentage** = (number affected ÷ total number) × 100.
**How many times higher** = larger risk ÷ smaller risk (for example 4.5 ÷ 0.5 = 9 times).
**Doubling:** cells after n divisions = 2 to the power n; useful values are 2^10 = 1024, 2^20 = 1 048 576 and 2^30 is about 1.07 billion.
A single cell dividing every day gives roughly a billion cells after about **30 days**, which shows why a tumour can become large quickly once it starts.
Read graphs carefully: check the **axis labels, units and scale** before comparing bars.
When describing a trend, give **figures with units**, for example 'rises from 0.5% to 4.5%'.
Round sensibly and give the unit, for example per 100 000 people, when the question uses it.
core.h: Calculations and data skills for cancer questions
core.p: This topic is a good source of maths marks. You may be asked to calculate **percentages**, **ratios** or **how many times higher** a risk is, to read **bar charts and tables**, or to use **powers of 2** for cell numbers. Showing your working is important: method marks are given even if the arithmetic slips. Always say what the numbers show in words after calculating.

bullets: **Mitosis and the cell cycle:** cancer is mitosis out of control; the cells do not stop at the end of the cycle.
**Mutation:** cancers start with changes in DNA; some mutations are caused by radiation and chemicals.
**Inheritance:** the BRCA example shows how alleles can raise risk.
**Non-communicable disease:** cancer is not caused by a pathogen and cannot be passed from person to person like an infection.
**Lifestyle:** the same behaviours (smoking, alcohol, obesity) are risk factors for several diseases, including heart disease.
**Screening and early detection** can find tumours before they spread, improving the chance of successful treatment.
**Treatment** (surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy) aims to remove or destroy the abnormal cells; the detail is beyond this spec point but good for context.
core.h: Cancer, the cell cycle and stem cells: links to other topics
core.p: Cancer is one of the best examples in GCSE biology of what goes wrong when the cell cycle is not controlled. It links to **mitosis** (the normal process being misused), to **stem cells** (which divide often and so are also affected by mutations) and to **inheritance** (mutations and alleles). It also links to **health**, because lifestyle choices such as smoking and diet are risk factors, and to **medicine and ethics**, because screening and treatment raise social and economic questions. Seeing these links lets you write extended answers that pull in more than one topic.

bullets: Use **'uncontrolled cell division'**, not just 'growing'.
Say **'spread to other parts of the body in the blood'**, not 'travels around the body'.
Write **'secondary tumours'** whenever you describe spread.
Never say benign tumours are 'not cancer cells' without saying they are **contained and do not invade**.
Use **'risk factor'** and 'increases the chance' rather than 'causes' unless asked for a cause.
Name examples: **smoking, UV, obesity, alcohol, BRCA1/BRCA2**.
In 6-mark answers, link **cells, genes, lifestyle and data** with a clear conclusion.
core.h: How to answer cancer questions: examiner's view
core.p: A top-grade answer is **precise with vocabulary** and links each statement to its reason. When asked about benign and malignant tumours, use the words **'invade'**, **'spread in the blood'** and **'secondary tumours'** for malignant, and **'contained in one area'**, **'membrane'** and **'do not invade'** for benign. When asked why people with a risk factor may not get cancer, say that risk factors only **increase the chance**. When asked to evaluate a claim, discuss **sample size, a control group, correlation versus causation, and a possible mechanism**.

exam: **State what cancer is (1 mark):** 'changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division' (the word 'uncontrolled' is essential).
**Describe a benign tumour (2 marks):** 'contained in one area, usually within a membrane' (1) and 'do not invade other parts of the body' (1).
**Describe a malignant tumour (2 to 3 marks):** invade neighbouring tissues (1); spread to other parts of the body in the blood (1); form secondary tumours (1).

**Compare benign and malignant (3 to 4 marks):** use 'whereas' to pair points: stays in one place v invades; no spread v spreads in blood; no secondary tumours v secondary tumours; not usually dangerous v dangerous.
**Explain why a malignant tumour is more dangerous (2 to 3 marks):** it spreads in the blood, forms secondary tumours in other organs, and is harder to remove or treat.
**Risk factor questions (1 to 2 marks):** name the factor and the cancer (smoking and lung cancer; UV and skin cancer); add 'increases the chance' rather than 'causes'.
**Genetic risk (2 marks):** 'inherited faulty BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene' (1) 'increases the risk of breast/ovarian cancer' (1).
**Data questions:** quote numbers with units from the chart or table, calculate 'how many times greater' by dividing, then state a conclusion in words.
**Evaluate a study (4 to 6 marks):** large sample, long period, control group, other variables controlled, correlation is not proof of causation, mechanism that explains the link, and a conclusion.
**Command words:** State = one fact; Describe = say what happens; Explain = give reasons (because); Compare = similarities and differences linked with 'whereas'; Evaluate = weigh up and conclude.
**6-mark answer plan:** (1) cancer defined, (2) benign, (3) malignant, (4) risk factors lifestyle and genetic, (5) data or evidence, (6) conclusion.

mistakes.r: Benign tumours are contained in one area, usually within a membrane, and do not invade other parts of the body.
mistakes.w: Benign tumours spread around the body.

mistakes.r: Cancer is caused by changes (mutations) in cells leading to uncontrolled growth and division; it is not communicable (some viruses only raise the risk).
mistakes.w: Cancer is caused by a bacterium or virus that you catch.

mistakes.r: Malignant cells spread to other parts of the body in the blood and form secondary tumours.
mistakes.w: Malignant tumours travel in the nerves.

mistakes.r: Smoking is a risk factor: it increases the chance of lung cancer but does not guarantee it.
mistakes.w: Smoking definitely causes lung cancer in everyone who smokes.

mistakes.r: Faulty BRCA1 or BRCA2 increases the risk of breast and ovarian cancer; it does not mean the cancer is certain.
mistakes.w: If you inherit BRCA1 you will get breast cancer.

mistakes.r: Cancer cells divide by mitosis, but out of control.
A tumour is a mass of abnormal cells; only malignant tumours are cancers, benign ones are not usually dangerous.
Cancer cells divide uncontrollably, so the number of cells increases; growth is by division.
mistakes.w: Cancer cells grow bigger and bigger.

mistakes.r: A correlation shows a link; scientists also need a mechanism and well-controlled studies to show a cause.
mistakes.w: A correlation between a factor and cancer proves the factor is the cause.

summary: AQA 4.2.2 (cancer): you must know that cancer is the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division, that benign tumours stay in one area (usually within a membrane) whereas malignant tumours invade neighbouring tissues and spread in the blood to form secondary tumours, and that both lifestyle and genetic risk factors exist. It matters because it combines cell division, mutation, health and data-interpretation skills, and appears in extended-response questions.

terms.d: The result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division.
A mass of abnormal cells produced by uncontrolled cell division.
A growth of abnormal cells which is contained in one area, usually within a membrane, and does not invade other parts of the body.
A tumour whose cells invade neighbouring tissues and spread to different parts of the body in the blood, forming secondary tumours.
A new tumour formed in another part of the body by cells that have spread from a malignant (primary) tumour.
The first tumour to form, at the original site where the cells began to divide in an uncontrolled way.
Cell division in which a cell divides to produce two genetically identical daughter cells.
A change in the sequence of bases in DNA.
A factor that is linked to an increased chance of developing a disease, but does not guarantee it.
A risk factor linked to behaviour or environment, such as smoking, obesity, alcohol or UV exposure.
An inherited gene or allele that increases the chance of developing a disease, for example faulty BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes and breast cancer.
A substance or type of radiation that can cause cancer, for example chemicals in tobacco smoke or ionising radiation.
Radiation such as X-rays and gamma rays that can damage DNA and cause mutations.
A disease that cannot be passed from one person to another, such as cancer.
The spread of cancer cells from a primary tumour to other parts of the body in the blood, where they form secondary tumours.
A relationship in which two variables change together; it does not by itself prove that one causes the other.
A cell that has become specialised for a particular function.

worked.ans: Smokers 4.5%, non-smokers 0.5%; the percentage is 9 times higher for smokers (so smoking is linked to a greater risk, not a certainty).
worked.q: In a study, 180 of 4000 smokers and 30 of 6000 non-smokers developed lung cancer. Calculate the percentage of each group who developed lung cancer and how many times higher the percentage is for smokers. (4 marks)
steps: State: smokers were 9 times as likely to develop lung cancer in this study.

worked.ans: Benign tumours are contained in one area, usually within a membrane, and do not invade or spread, so they do not form secondary tumours and are not usually dangerous. Malignant tumours invade neighbouring tissue, and cells spread in the blood to other parts of the body where they form secondary tumours, so they are dangerous.
worked.q: Describe the differences between a benign tumour and a malignant tumour. (4 marks)
steps: Benign cells are contained in one area, usually within a membrane, whereas malignant cells invade neighbouring tissues.
Benign tumours do not spread to other parts of the body, but malignant cells spread in the blood.
Malignant tumours form secondary tumours in other organs, but benign tumours do not.
Benign tumours are not usually dangerous, whereas malignant tumours (cancers) are.

worked.ans: The faulty gene only increases the chance of breast cancer; it does not guarantee it. Cancer also depends on other mutations occurring and on lifestyle and environmental factors, so she may never develop it.
worked.q: A woman has an inherited faulty BRCA1 gene. Explain why she may still not develop breast cancer. (3 marks)
steps: The faulty gene is a risk factor, so it increases the chance of cancer rather than making it certain.
Cancer needs mutations that cause uncontrolled cell division; these may not occur.
Lifestyle and environment also affect the risk, so an interaction of factors decides the outcome.
